items.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]

ctx.x: And he’d just hit them all. And you’d go oh, there they are. And you’d know if it was a D minor chord you’d hear D minor, and then you’d hear down the line D minor, C and you’d hear it all going. And you’d just sit there and he’d go, “you got it?” And he would look at me like you got it. And I’d go oh, okay. And I was so happy that he was being nice to me. And so, that was in Odessa in 1981 I think. Herb Ellis couldn’t make it and my father says, “we’ll take the kid, we’ll take him down there.” And so I found…
Well how does a young player who doesn’t have the advantage of having a father like that, do the ear thing, like you did it?

items.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: And oh, Bucky Pizzarelli’s son John, John Pizzarelli. He’s kind of a star now, he sings, you know, he’s getting really popular. And he plays real good.

ctx.x: So who is a guitarist — name a couple of guitarists on the scene that you see coming up that are continuing to breathe life into guitar playing.

Al Cohn’s son, Joe Cohn plays very well. And oh, Bucky Pizzarelli’s son John, John Pizzarelli. He’s kind of a star now, he sings, you know, he’s getting really popular. And he plays real good. And if I think of any more, there are a lot of them but I just, I don’t keep them readily at hand anyway. That’s about all I know about everything.
Well I just would like to ask you then, if you would give us a word of wisdom, if you had a word to say to young guitarists coming up, wanting to involve themselves in this music. What would it be?
